anchors.fact: In 1731 Ashley leased a large old tavern on Ludgate Hill and renamed it for four things at once: coffee house, punch house, Dorchester beer, Welsh ale (Oxford ASHLEY pdf 160; F2).
anchors.meaning: The whole thing laid out before the doors opened, every trade in its place.
anchors.speaksTo: holds the whole thing at once

anchors.fact: He had extensive cellars, bought his spirits in large lots and aged them himself, and that is why the punch could be cheap (Oxford pdf 162; F11).
anchors.meaning: The part nobody drinking upstairs ever saw is what made it work for them. The page ties the cellars to the low price, not to anything else.

anchors.fact: By the evidence of his advertisements (Oxford calls it circumstantial), every punch was made from a shrub of sour Seville-orange peel and juice, premixed, bottled and kept in the cellar; Oxford's SHRUB entry says he sold it too, up to whole hogsheads (pdf 162, 1793–1794; F12–F13, C1).
anchors.meaning: The one piece prepared in full before the evening starts, so that nothing during it has to be thought out again. Labelled "it seems". Say "bottled and cellared", never "made before anyone asked" (G3).

anchors.fact: Because of the shrub, his bartenders could make punch of any size as fast as a glass of wine is poured, and the house was always crowded: big, well placed, good and cheap (Oxford pdf 162; F14–F15).
anchors.meaning: Everyone else got speed and ease; the crowd never had to think about why it worked. The speed comes from the shrub, not from mixing in front of the customer (C3).
anchors.speaksTo: a whole room gets to be carefree because one person held it all

anchors.fact: Oxford's PUNCH entry corrects itself: Ashley, "or rather" his chief barkeeper Mrs. Gaywood and the young women under her, put each drink together in front of the guest (pdf 1328; ASHLEY pdf 162; F8–F9).
anchors.meaning: The plan was his; the cups went through other people's hands (Oxford's "or rather"), and it held. Never "every cup" or "weren't his" as an absolute (audit v2 R2–R3). Never "Ashley mixed every cup"; "Catherine" only with "perhaps" (C2, C7).
anchors.speaksTo: the piece they didn't place (pieces that are people)

anchors.fact: Before long, the coffee, beer and ale stopped being central, and the house was known simply as the London Punch House (Oxford pdf 160; F3).
anchors.meaning: Of the four things he planned, one became what the house was known for. Who or what moved it isn't on the page (audit v2 R4–R6); "made it famous" only under "I like to think". The page is passive: who called it that, and why, is our reading, signposted (L2). Told as what people came for, never as a name the public took (Wren's ruling 1).
anchors.speaksTo: fear: the one piece that moves on its own; it may be what people came for

anchors.fact: For a time in the 1750s he handed the bar to his son and dealt in spirits from his cellars; when he died in 1776 he was back running the bar, with his son (Oxford pdf 163; F19).
anchors.meaning: The hidden truth, gently funny: the planner never quite stood behind the counter as a guest of his own house. No motive on the page: one "I like to think…" only (L3). Never "retired", "took it back" or "couldn't let go" (G7).
anchors.speaksTo: rarely gets to simply be in what they built

anchors.fact: He had an inscription painted across the front of the house telling how he'd lowered the price of punch and made it popular, "Pro Bono Publico", for the public good (Oxford pdf 163; F18).
anchors.meaning: His mark was about what the public got. Once, neutrally (Wren's ruling 5); never "obsessed", never the lawsuits.

anchors.fact: Oxford: he pioneered and popularised mixing spirits to order in single portions, and is responsible, "perhaps" more than anyone, for the modern bar (pdf 160; F17).
anchors.meaning: One clause, hedge kept (C4). Never a chain handed down (*Down the Line*).
anchors.speaksTo: the proposal (what a well-built thing carries)

anchors.fact: Batavia arrack: a pungent, intensely flavoured Indonesian spirit, mostly of sugar cane and rice (palm sap contested, C8); the dearest spirit he made punch with (6s a quart, against 4s for brandy or rum), and not to everyone's taste (Oxford ARRACK pdf 147, 149; ASHLEY pdf 162; A1, A3, F6).
anchors.meaning: The one piece with a will of its own inside an ordered cup (Wren's thought; Tomás's call). Never "first on his price list" (C6).

cocktail.closingLine: The arrack stays the loudest thing in the glass. When something tonight moves by itself, let it surprise you too.
cocktail.glassware: glass punch cup with a handle (about 200 ml), no ice
method: The day before, peel the orange thinly: just the coloured part, none of the white.
Rub the peel into the sugar with your fingers, cover, and leave it about 12 hours. The sugar pulls the oil out of the peel.
Squeeze the juice, stir it into the sugar until it has dissolved, and strain out the peel. Bottle it and keep it in the fridge (it keeps up to ten days), with a bottle of water beside it.

To serve: pour the arrack, shrub and cold water straight into the cup, give it a few turns of a spoon, and hand it over. That's one part spirit to two of everything else. There's no ice, so it tastes exactly as you measured it.
cocktail.name: Built to Hold

preparations.text: the peel of 1 Seville orange, 80 g demerara sugar and 250 ml fresh Seville orange juice (5 or 6 oranges). Seville oranges come in winter. The rest of the year, use the peel of 1 ordinary orange, 75 ml orange juice and 175 ml lemon juice.
preparations.title: The shrub (about 300 ml, enough for seven cups)

recipe.item: Batavia arrack (from Java; about 50%: check the label), recommended, or a full-flavoured Jamaican-style rum of 50% or stronger
recipe.note: Not Sri Lankan arrack, which is made from coconut palm. Keep it in the fridge.
Bottled the day before; from the fridge.
From a bottle kept in the fridge.

cocktail.tagline: They get the surprise. You built the room it happens in.

reading.epigraph: From 1731, a London house made punch as quickly as wine is poured. Roughly like this.
whoYouAre: You're the one holding all of it. The trip, the move, the wedding, the project at work: you know where every piece is, who arrives when, what happens if the train's late, and how each part leans on the others. Everyone else just turns up, and it works. Some of them call it luck.

You don't mention it, but the evening has already happened once, in your head, every way it could go wrong. And while everyone else enjoys it, part of you is still on duty, watching for the one thing you didn't put there: the guest nobody told you about, the plan someone quietly changed, the piece that moves by itself. You watch because it would mean something in your world had a mind of its own.

It gives people more than they know. Because you hold all of it, the rest of them can put it down. A whole room gets to be carefree for a night, and that's your doing. It's worth every minute you spent on duty.
yours: In 1731, James Ashley took the lease of a big old tavern on Ludgate Hill, in London, and renamed it for four things at once: coffee, punch, beer and ale. He had extensive cellars, where he aged spirits bought in large lots. By his advertisements and accounts of the bar, it seems every punch began from the same base: a shrub of sour Seville-orange peel and juice, bottled and kept in the cellar. With that ready, any amount of punch could be made as quickly as wine is poured. The house was always crowded.

The hands at the counter were mostly someone else's. His chief bartender, Mrs. Gaywood, and the young women under her put each drink together in front of the guest. The plan was his, the cups went through other people's hands, and it held. Something else moved too, and who moved it is anyone's guess. Before long the coffee, beer and ale stopped being the heart of the business, and the place was known simply as the London Punch House. Of the four things he'd planned, one became what the house was known for.

Then the bit I can't help smiling at. In the 1750s he handed the bar to his son and turned to dealing in spirits from his cellars. When he died, in 1776, he was back running the bar, with his son. Maybe his son asked him to. I like to think he missed holding it. You'd understand that. And I like to think you'd see what I see in his house: the pieces he didn't hold himself, the hands at the counter and the trade that outgrew the other three, were what made it famous.

His recipe is lost, so the cocktail I've made for you is mine, built from what's known of his: one part spirit to two of everything else, which was his standard, and, it seems, a Seville-orange shrub. The spirit is Batavia arrack, from Java, distilled mostly from cane and rice: pungent, full of flavour, and the dearest spirit he made punch with. I chose it as the loud piece, the one with a will of its own. What holds it is the shrub: orange peel rubbed into sugar until the oil comes out, then the juice, bottled and kept cold, with a bottle of water beside it. Arrack, shrub and cold water go straight into the cup, a few turns of a spoon, no ice. It's sharp, bright and warm at once, and the arrack still sounds clearly through it. The order doesn't quiet the loud part. It gives it somewhere to stand.

Keep holding it all: everyone near you is lucky you do. But next time a piece moves by itself, a guest you didn't plan for or a change you weren't warned about, don't put it back at once. Give it the evening. What you built is stronger than you fear, and the piece that moved may turn out to be the part everyone remembers. And you'd finally get to be surprised by your own world, like everyone else in it.
